findings.issue_category: hardcoded cloud credentials in user data
findings.description: The EC2 user_data script exports a static AWS access key ID and secret access key in plaintext. Instance metadata/user-data is readable by anyone with access to the instance (and to anyone able to read the Terraform state or code), leaking long-lived IAM credentials.
The security group allows TCP port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing SSH administration to the entire internet and enabling brute-force or exploit attempts against the instance.
The egress rule permits all protocols and ports to 0.0.0.0/0, allowing a compromised instance to exfiltrate data or reach command-and-control endpoints without restriction.
No metadata_options block is set, so IMDSv1 remains enabled. Combined with a public web server this permits SSRF-based theft of instance credentials from the metadata service.
The instance defines no root_block_device with encrypted = true, so the root EBS volume may be stored unencrypted at rest.
The instance is launched in a public subnet with map_public_ip_on_launch enabled and an internet gateway default route, placing it directly on the internet rather than behind a load balancer or NAT.
The EBS volume does not set encrypted = true, so data written to the attached disk is stored unencrypted and readable from raw snapshots or underlying storage.
The snapshot is taken from an unencrypted EBS volume, so the backup copy of the data is also unencrypted at rest.
The VPC flow log destination bucket has no server-side encryption configuration, so sensitive network traffic metadata is stored unencrypted.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block or ACL/policy restriction is defined for the flow log bucket, leaving it vulnerable to accidental public exposure of network logs.
force_destroy = true with no versioning or object lock means flow log evidence can be silently deleted or overwritten, undermining audit integrity during incident response.
map_public_ip_on_launch = true causes every instance in this subnet to receive a public IP, exposing workloads to the internet by default.
